[GAVEL] Good afternoon, and Happy Black History Month to everyone. I am Council Member Althea Stevens, Chair of New York City Council Committee on Children and Youth. Before we begin, I want to take a moment to thank Commissioner Dannhauser for his years of dedicated service. Will you give him a round of applause, too, because I don't, I'd be all clapping and stuff up in here. I'm not supposed to, but I think it is due for someone who has been a dedicated servant, a dedicated leader and administrator of the Children and Services. Over many years and across different divisions at ACS, he has shown a deep commitment to children and families

of New York City. We are grateful for your leadership and the care he has brought to this work, and we wish him all the very best in his next chapter. We really appreciate the work that you've done. I mean, you can always tell when there's a provider leading agencies because the care that they bring to it. No shade to nobody else, but I have a special place in my heart for providers. Thank you for joining us today on our oversight hearing entitled Examining Racial Disparities in the Child Welfare System. We will also be considering the following three bills amending and advancing family rights, improving services for children, and involved in the child welfare system. Introduction 242, I mean 424, I don't know why I kept saying 2, 424 sponsored by Council Member Pierina Sanchez would require the Commission of Health and Mental Hygiene to establish and operate a pilot program providing free mental health services to children who've been returned to their homes following removal; Introduction 449, sponsored by myself, requiring child protective specialists to provide certain information verbally to parents or other legal responsible caregivers at the first point

of contact during an investigation of an alleged child abuse or malnutrition; Introduction 466, sponsored by Council Member Ung, which would require ACS to produce multilingual disclosures from distinguished citywide languages and make it available during a child protective investigation on its website. For decades, oversight bodies advocated and impacted families have documented racial disparities in our child welfare system. Black and Latinx families are more likely to be reported to State Central Registry, more likely to be investigated, and more likely to experience a trauma of child removals and foster care placement. In 2021, ACS began implementing structural changes in part intended to confront these inequalities. These efforts included shifting towards family-based foster settings, strengthening preventative services, and expanding supports for parents and caregivers, enhancing mental health services, and reducing unnecessary reports through mandated reporting education. These efforts are commendable and represent important steps forward.

However, ACS' own data demonstrates that significant disparities persist. In Fiscal Year 2025, Black children were overrepresented in emergency removals and foster care entries compared to the share of SCR intakes. Hispanic children also continue to experience disproportionate involvement in key decision points. By contrast, White children were underrepresented in removals and foster care entries relative to their share of reports. These patterns raise serious questions about decision-making throughout the system and whether recent reforms are translating into more equitable outcomes. Today, we look forward to hearing from ACS about the progress being made, the measurable impact of those reforms, and additional steps needed to ensure fairness at steps within the child welfare system. The legislation being heard today builds on the agency's reform efforts and is intended to further support the City's shared goals of protecting children while strengthening and preserving families whenever it is safe to do so. I'd like to thank the Committee Staff for their hard work in preparing for this hearing, as well as all of my team back in the sweet 16. I mean,

they keep removing the names because I say them wrong, but I can say Elizabeth Arzt, so thank you for your work. And Rie, what's your last name?
Ogasawara.
What?
Ogasawara.
Ogasawara.
Yeah.

Oh, look at that. I said your name. Y'all can put your names back in. I can say the names. With that, I will turn it over to Committee Staff to swear in our first panel, and I believe CORE is our first panel. I know you've been here a long time, so we're going to get you in here, so you can go. She had a hearing earlier today, too, so.

Thank you. We will now hear testimony from the Administration. Before we begin, I will administer the affirmation. Please raise your right hand. I will read the affirmation once, then call on you to respond. Do you affirm to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth before this

Committee, and to respond honestly to Council Member questions?
I do.
Thank you.

Thank you. Good morning, Chair Stevens and Members of the Children and Youth Committee. My name is Linda Tigani, and I have the honor of serving as the Chair and Executive Director for the New York City Commission on Racial Equity. I lead CORE in partnership with 13 commissioners and 15 staff members. New York City CORE is the product of a 2022 ballot measure to enshrine in the City Charter a commitment to redressing longstanding racial disparities in power, access, and opportunity enabled and perpetuated, whether by design, implementation, or impact through City law, regulation, policies, and practices. To approach this goal, the Racial Justice Commission proposed that a body be established for the purpose of holding government accountable, for advancing racial equity, and increasing community voices to influence City decision-making through the development of priorities for racial equity in government operation. New York City CORE exercises

this accountability function first and foremost through oversight of a citywide racial equity plan outlining goals and strategies for reducing racial disparities in social and economic well-being, and we look forward to reviewing the plan developed by the Administration for Children's Services. Collectively, the 2022 Charter amendments represent an understanding that the benefits and burdens of government policies are not evenly distributed across racial groups, and few systems illustrate these disparities as starkly as child welfare. In fulfilling its central mandate to propose equity priorities and outcome indicators based on needs identified by New Yorkers harmed by racism and social injustice, New York City CORE spoke with parents and children who experience ACS as punitive rather than supportive and driven by personal and institutional biases instead of genuine concerns for safety. To them, and I agree, the child welfare system is effectively a civil counterpart to the criminal legal system, both in the degree of discretion it affords and the potential for abuse of that authority. In fact, it was at the urging of community members that NYC CORE expanded a racial

equity priority pertaining to holding law enforcement accountable for abuse of power and harm they commit to include child welfare personnel. Community members impacted by the system have reported not only being targeted for lacking the means to meet their children's needs, but also being profiled by virtue of their race, a perspective all too consistent with data revealing that almost 45 percent of Black and Latinx children experience an investigation by age 18, and that Black and Latinx families do account for 90 percent of system-involved families despite constituting only 60 percent of the city's child population. By ACS' own account, Black families compared to other families were disproportionately separated, less likely to be mandated to receive additional services instead of removal, and experienced longer stays in the foster care system. The carceral approach taken by ACS can be traced back to chattel slavery, Jim Crow, and the legacy of slavery, which will be addressed in NYC CORE's forthcoming work in reparations, truth healing, and reconciliation. Although neglect allegations which drive the vast share of cases are meant to be reserved for

parents who fail to provide for their children despite having the means to do so, families report being separated due to challenges meeting such basic needs as housing, food, and child care. Meanwhile, funding that might support the fulfillment of these needs is invested in a foster care system that consistently yields negative mental health, education, and socioeconomic outcomes. NYC CORE is also charged with responding to requests from City Council and other government officials, and we're honored to have been identified by former Deputy Mayor Anne Williams-Isom as a government partner to Narrowing the Front Door Working Group in its efforts to advance the recommendations from its 2022 report on stemming the pipeline into the child welfare system. I'm pleased to share that these recommendations have recently yielded resolution 153-2026 calling on the City to acknowledge the harm caused by a system conceded by ACS itself to be marred by racism and classism and to commit to making more equitable policy and funding choices moving forward. As the City's racial equity oversight body, NYC CORE is united with Narrowing the Front Door in

the understanding that our government leaders, elected and non-elected, must acknowledge the City's role in perpetuating these harms and commit to a path of healing that truth-telling processes and restorative practices teach us as possible. To support this course correction, NYC CORE joins Narrowing the Front Door in its call for a community-run accountability council ideally established by law and funded by City government entrusted with developing a roadmap for reducing family investigation and separation and investing in the health and well-being of Black and Latinx children and families including those currently in the foster care system. Through such fact-gathering activities as data collection and analysis, focus groups and public hearings, the council would identify corrective action steps and future initiatives to end the harms of the current system and redress past harms and prevent future harms. Finally, NYC CORE echoes Narrowing the Front Door's recommendation that City Council support the provision of direct, unrestricted financial support to families independently of the child welfare system. Hold ACS accountable for the racial

disparities in the system and for the poor outcomes for youth in foster care. Collaborate with advocates to develop agency data and budget transparency requirements. Dismantle pipelines to the foster system that fuel racial disparities including mandated reporter laws and hospital drug testing. Use discretionary funds to support community-based services as a foundation for community and family-centered system of care. Fund attorneys and advocates trained to support families with education issues. And pass the parents' Miranda's bill requiring ACS to inform parents of their rights including their right to an attorney at the start of an investigation. New York City CORE thanks Chair Stevens for her stewardship of the latter bill as well as resolution 153-2026, and we look forward to working together to facilitate its swift passage. I close with an invitation to City Council, ACS, and City Hall to partner with New York City CORE in its ongoing efforts to realize a city in which Black and Latinx children are raised by their parents and within their families in a city where the Black family is honored, respected, and able to live

a life filled with joy, peace, and prosperity. Thank you.

Thank you. I would like to acknowledge Council Member Felder, Williams, and Joseph. I have a couple of questions for you. What reforms are necessary to meaningfully reduce disparities in children removals and investigations? I know you mentioned some of them in your statement around like direct supports to families, but could you go in detail as to what other reforms you believe would help with some of this work?

Sure. The statement goes into detail to uplift the reforms that were identified by Narrowing the Front Door, and I just want to first offer that those reforms take the center stage for CORE. One, because they were identified and created by people directly impacted so parents and foster care families and institutions that work with people who are directly impacted by the system. Any reform that we move forward with as a City must center their voices. We have worked very closely with them to develop a accountability council that would be community led, include 13 people which

would have representation from all five boroughs as well as youth voice representation from all five boroughs and really put power, access, and opportunity in the hands of those impacted to provide policy recommendations, and CORE would act as both the home of the council so we would provide operational support and the funding would go through us but we think that it is best and important and a sign of actually like true investment in Black and Latinx families that City government provide the full funding for this council. So, we would bring together government leaders because we know that children go into the child welfare system, families go into the child welfare system by several pathways, everyone from schools to hospitals to Department of Probation to sometimes like our local counselors. And so we are taking a whole of government approach to ensure that the community members that would come on to the council through a public process would be directly supported by CORE as well as Narrowing the Front Door that created, they conceptualized this particular council which to our understanding would be the first of its kind in the nation, and then they would develop the policy recommendations, they would look

at the data with CORE staff. I also want to uplift the Miranda Rights Bill which is essential for families. There's no reason anyone in this country should not be told what their rights are from the start of an investigation. It is an affront to both our constitutional rights as well as what we claim we are as a city in our New York City Charter. And I also want to uplift the support for provision of direct and unrestricted financial support. We see a lot of cases are coming through the pipeline particularly because Black parents are being criminalized for being parents and Black parents are being criminalized for being poor and poverty is a systemic issue. We created it as a nation, we created it as a city. And so unrestricted funds that look like a universal basic income program for anyone who is experiencing struggle with respect to housing, food, or education is essential, and that would go so far as to ensuring that students who are experiencing investigations, families who are experiencing investigations then have the actual support that they need to be the parents that they truly are, but the system is preventing them from being that.

And I know even in your recommendations, and I know you said like working with Narrowing the Front Door, and I think I heard you say something about like the youth, but how do you also make sure that young people's voices are also being heard? That is very important to me in this process because I feel like a lot of times adults are often talking around young people and they're also part of this process, and so how are they being integrated into this work and how do we keep that separate and have the integrity of young people's voices to also guide this work in policymaking?

So, hopefully when established, the accountability council will have 13 seats, three of which would be reserved for interdisciplinary experts, and then 10 will be reserved for two seats per borough, one seat for an adult and one seat for a young person. We are also going to be leveraging the community engagement process work that the New York City Commission on Racial Equity does for our own engagement. Right now, we've completed a second cycle that yielded just short of 10,000 voices and those voices include

people as young as 11 years old. And this particular topic and conversation was raised to CORE by the public in our first engagement cycle when we worked with 4,212 New Yorkers. And the way that community phrased it was they said we want a CCRB but for ACS. And then former Deputy Mayor Anne Williams-Isom introduced us to both Jess Dannhauser as well as Narrowing the Front Door, and Narrowing the Front Door shared that community members have already conceptualized what this can look like and they needed a government partner. And that's really what CORE is set up to do. It's to be able to partner with members of the public, whether they're in an organization or not, and be able to bring the public solutions to public policy challenges to bear and bring government as well as community together. And we've been in conversation with ACS. We've gotten a lot of support from Commissioner Dannhausner. And we've worked hand in hand with Narrowing the Front Door. And the last thing I'll say is in every single event we've done partnering with Narrowing the Front Door, young people have always been centered. Their youth voices have always been in the room. We

did have a public session where we introduced the accountability council model to the public to say before we bring this deeper into government, we wanted to make sure more community voices were a part of it. And young people were in the room and also participated and engaged and were asking the same questions you were asking. And so we went back in to say, well, we have a model that brings up youth voices. We also want to make sure that they are at the table to influence the decisions that the council will make.

Yeah, no. That's always going to be my first response because in this work, people are always talking around children, and young people are never the ones kind of coming up with these solutions and, you know, we're supposed to support them so that's always going to be something that I'm fighting for and pushing for and making sure is happening in government because it happens all the time. So, that's very important to me and a priority to make sure, especially as we're talking about bringing in community, that community is also young people because we're also talking about diversity,

but sometimes we forget that young people should be a part of that. My next question is, and I know my Colleagues had a question as well. So what extent are poverty and housing instability and mandating reporting practices contributing to racial disparities in child wealth and involvement? Do you have any statistics or any of those things that, because I know you guys have been working on that as well.

So, I have the statistics that I had raised in my particular testimony, but I'm happy to follow up with a deeper report outlining what and how poverty is showing up in particular cases. I do just want to honor that folks, I know there are plenty of people who are also going to be testifying to that data. I think what's important to note is that there is a particular criminalization of poverty within the Black community that does not exist in other communities. And so it's both, well, where are we seeing our community members who are not able to make affordable housing prices, which we are now seeing are actually in no way, shape, or form affordable for New Yorkers, that when

our families are being judged by their income, something that they really cannot control, prices that they're forced to pay also that they cannot control. There's an added piece of criminality that comes into the decision-making process. And that's not something that is new. This is, again, what we are seeing as a growth from chattel slavery to Jim Crow. Now we are living in the legacy of slavery. And so, as the reforms are being made, we're really not thinking as critically as we can about what role poverty is playing in these decisions and how are we looking at poverty differently from when it's a White family to when it's a Black family to when it's a Latinx family.
Is the Commission examining the roles of other City agencies like DOE, NYPD, DYCD in contributing to the disproportionate reports of Black and Latinx families?

Yes. So, those are some of the agencies that we imagine will be a part of the corresponding government council that will be working and hearing from the accountability council, and this is the whole of government approach. We also believe that OMB should be on that

list and any agency, which includes DYCD, that is working with a parent or with a child, with a foster care institution. It includes agencies that work with preventative services, investigative services, and so we really do need the broader City government agencies at the table to do this work.

Since 2021 foster care redesign, ACS has launched intensive initiatives, including family enrichment centers, peer parent and advocates, extended therapeutic services, expansion of CARES track. From the Commission's perspective, have any of the reforms measurable reduce racial disparities? And does the Commission believe any of those strategies warrant further investigation or scaling up?

So, we are in the process right now of doing further investigation on all of those strategies. I will say we have worked as a Commission for the community equity priority process. We did work with family enrichment centers. We have spoken with the ACS leadership team about this work. But we also consistently go out and talk to community. And what I would like to raise is that we are hearing and seeing two very different things.

I think we are seeing some of the data shifting very slightly, but shifting, and we are seeing policy reform. But when we go out and we talk to children and parents, that is not their experience of ACS, and it is not their experience of what it means to be Black and Latinx in community. And so what CORE is doing right now is looking to see how our community-centered research approach will be leveraged in the forthcoming accountability council because we need to make both a clarity but also a bridge between what the data is telling us on a quantitative side and what communities are telling us that they experience. The last thing I will note is that in our investigations, we have found that a consistent problem is that all of the data is not made publicly available, the data that we would need to be able to make these determinations, and that when data is made available, there is a lag between the data that should be coming to us right now and then the data that is produced by the City. That is not just on ACS. It is a citywide problem. But as we know, we need to be looking at the child welfare system as a whole-of-government approach that has been taken

against Black and Latinx families that should be in support of Black and Latinx families, and so we need to look at the data across several agencies.
Does any of my colleagues have questions? All right. Well, that is all I have for this panel. Thank you for coming in today, and we appreciate your work.
Thank you so much. Thank you, everyone.
So, we'll call our next panel, I believe, which is

Good afternoon. Panelists, please raise your right hand. I will read the affirmation once, then call on each of you individually to respond. Do you affirm to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth before this Committee and to respond honestly to Council Member questions?
I do.
I do.

I do.
Thank you.
I'm going to let it slide, but you've got like 35 pages here for your testimony.
A lot of them are data. A lot of it's data. It's not all…
I'm going to let it slide because it's your last hearing with me.
It's only 13 pages of actual testimony.
13 is a lot.
I'll go fast. I'll go fast.
But again, it's your last hearing, so I'm going to let you do your thing.

Thank you, Chair Stevens. Good afternoon to Chair Stevens, Council Member Joseph, Deputy Speaker Williams. My name is Jess Dannhauser, and I'm honored and privileged to be the Commissioner of the Administration for Children's Services. I'm joined today by Winette Saunders, the First Deputy Commissioner; Elvita Dominique, the Executive Director of Equity Strategies at ACS; and

Ina Mendez, the Deputy Commissioner for Family Permanency Services. Thank you, Chair Stevens and Members of the Children and Youth Committee for holding today's oversight hearing. Good to be with you as well, Council Member Felder. Examining racial disparities in the child welfare system. This is a critically important topic and one that I, as well as my team at ACS, have been focused on throughout my four years as ACS Commissioner. ACS' mission is to protect the children of New York City, a mission we take with the utmost seriousness. Over the last several years, having listened to youth and families with lived experience and learned a great deal from the pandemic, we have expanded our perspective on what this means. ACS is responsible for both ensuring children are safe in their homes and safe from harms that can come from unnecessary system involvement. In our effort to achieve both of these vital goals, we have carried out a comprehensive set of initiatives. As always, there is more to do. I think it is important to start by sharing the data with you. I'll walk you through some of the data, and we're also including data slides at

the end of this testimony. As you know, if someone suspects a child is being abused or maltreated, they should make a report to the New York Statewide Central Register. When the State accepts a report about a New York City child, ACS responds to assess the safety of that child. In 2024, a Black child was eight times more likely to be in an SCR report than a White child. A Hispanic child was six times more likely in an SCR report and investigation than a White child. More than 82 percent of the families experiencing an ACS child protection response were Black or Hispanic in 2024. In 2024, a Black child in an investigation was 1.18 times more likely to be in an indicated investigation than a White child. A Hispanic child was 1.26 times more likely to be in an indicated investigation than a White child. These ratios have been stubbornly similar over many years. This is similar at every stage of involvement, including court involvement and placement in foster care. However, what has changed is that today, far fewer families are involved in a child protection response to an SCR report. The number declined 16 percent from 2017 to 2024, from about 51,000 to about 43,000. For Hispanic families, this was a 3 percent

decrease. For Black families, this was a 19 percent decrease. For White families, this was a 25 percent decrease. And for Asian families, it was a 4 percent decrease. Even more dramatically, the number of families experiencing an indicated investigation fell 46 percent between 2017 and 2024, from 19,361 to 10,420 families. For Hispanic families, this was a 36 percent decrease. For Black families, this was a 51 percent decrease. And for White families, this was a 56 percent decrease. For Asian families, it was a 41 percent decrease. This reduction in half is significant for families, as having an indicated case can have longstanding ramifications, including when seeking employment. Similarly, in that period, the number of families experiencing court-ordered supervision declined 63 percent, from 5,160 to about 1,900. For Hispanic families, this was a 55 percent decrease. For Black families, this was a 68 percent decrease. For White families, it was a 77 percent decrease. And for Asian families, this was a 68 percent decrease. And the number of court filings seeking foster care of abused and neglected children declined 37 percent, from 2017 to 2024, from 1,959 to 1,227. For Black families, this was a 38 percent

decrease. For Hispanic families, it was a 32 percent decrease. For White families, it was a 60 percent decrease. And for Asian families, it was a 44 percent decrease. In sum, we have significantly reduced the likelihood of unnecessary system involvement, yet serious disparities remain, which require continued urgent attention. Throughout my time as Commissioner, we have been intentional about working to reduce unnecessary reports to the SCR, thus reducing unnecessary child protection responses, while increasing family access to community-based supports without the need for an SCR report. For the past three years, ACS has been working closely with other City agencies and systems to make better use of the State's Child Abuse and Neglect Hotline and to provide earlier and more effective support for families without the need for an SCR report or child protection response. Since January 2023, we've collaborated with New York City Public Schools, Health and Hospitals, Department of Homeless Services, the Department of Health and Mental Hygiene, the Mayor's Office to End Gender-Based Violence, and dozens of private hospitals, charter

schools, and social service organizations to educate mandated reporters on how to help families get the help they might need without calling the Child Abuse Hotline, except when children are truly not safe. In total, the ACS team has conducted over 435 presentations, reaching over 27,000 mandated reporters. Entitled, The Evolving Focus of Child Welfare, Addressing Overreporting, and Providing Family Center Supports, the sessions provide guidance on when a report to the SCR is necessary and when it is not. We explain the shift underway in New York State, which has moved its messaging, thanks to advocacy from many in this room, to mandated reporters from when in doubt, call the SCR, to you can support a family without having to report a family when maltreatment is not suspected. Our sessions provide detailed information on ACS funded and other supports and services available to families in New York City and ways to build towards a culture shift from reporting to supporting families with successful engagement, relationship building, and access to services. Many sessions include presentations by local ACS funded community-based organizations. As a result, we have seen a reduction

in reports and an increase in supports accessed without the SCR. For example, in the past two years, 2025 compared to 2023, SCR reports from schools have decreased by 16 percent, social service agencies by 16 percent as well, and health and mental health personnel, mostly in hospitals, by 7 percent. In 2025, ACS received approximately 5,000 fewer reports from these three sectors than it did in 2023. The ACS support line now receives more than 4,000 calls per year from families themselves and from schools and others who are working directly with families. Formally created in November 2023, the ACS support line has the sole purpose of supporting the community through engagement and connections to resources, prevention services, and our concrete services. The support line now receives an average of more than 300 inquiries per month, up from about 30 monthly in early 2023. This increase is attributed to the ongoing work to ensure our community partners and families are made aware of how to access prevention services and other resources outside of the child welfare system in New York City. With regard to family support services, we have been very intentional about our efforts to

ensure families and colleagues are accessing these services through community referrals and not just after a child protective investigation. These efforts are working, with more to do. Community referrals have increased from 12 percent of prevention referrals in January 2023 to 25 percent in December 2025. These past four years, we've also focused on efforts to provide services and supports to families as upstream as possible so that they never need to come into contact with the child protection system. This includes the launch of the school-based early support program, the expansion of low-income child care vouchers, the expansion of family enrichment centers from three to 30 citywide, and our ongoing child safety campaigns, each of which I will briefly summarize. Launched in 2024, the school-based early support prevention model is aimed at providing families with services and supports as upstream as possible, preventing involvement with child protection while keeping children safe. Each of the 16 new programs are required to partner with at least three elementary and middle schools to help families address stressors that may impact their well-being,

help families access concrete items, and strengthen social connections within the school communities. The model also includes a community pathway track that's funded solely by CTL that does not require opening a formal prevention case. Starting in 2022, ACS rapidly expanded child care assistance for low-income families, providing vouchers that cover most or all the costs of child care. This initiative has made child care affordable for thousands more families across New York City. Between the summer of '22 and the summer of '25, the number of children enrolled in care with the support of an ACS-issued low-income voucher climbed by 900 percent, from 7,400 to more than 75,000. During this period, ACS has also expanded access in communities historically underserved by the program, namely the 17 community districts with the highest poverty unemployment rates that have faced inadequate access to child care. The number from these neighborhoods enrolled in care with a low-income voucher increased from just 1,500 to nearly 22,000, a 1,300 percent increase. We also increased support for families and communities by expanding family enrichment centers from three to 30.

In fact, the contract for the 30th FEC just started this past January. As you know, FECs are welcoming family-centered spaces co-designed with parents, caregivers, and community members to be places where families with children come together. No two FECs are alike, as they reflect the culture, strengths, and identity of its neighborhood. The ACS Office of Child Safety and Injury Prevention focuses on reducing unintentional child injuries among children, such as safe sleep, medication safety, and window guards. The office is often out in communities sharing information and building awareness among caregivers and child-serving professionals. ACS does this work with an understanding that there can be fear associated with our involvement. In addition to significant efforts to make our services more accessible, ACS is supportive of efforts to create solutions outside of ACS that obviate the need for child protective involvement. In fact, it was going to be earlier today, but it will be tomorrow, along with Deputy Mayor Arteaga and our colleagues at DOHMH, Luisa Linares, is going to announce Strong Foundations, a new partnership with

ACS is providing the Health Department with 20 million dollars over three years so they can expand and enhance clinical infrastructure and the continuum of perinatal newborn and early childhood services without the need for ACS involvement with the family. The funding will enable the Health Department to expand eligibility for nurse-family partnership called NFPx to pregnant people in their third trimester and up until the birth of the child and for those with more than one child, which has been a serious limitation before more families will be able to access this. The new partnership also expands capacity in their perinatal and early child mental health clinics and expands DOHMH training and technical assistance in perinatal mental health to build the capacity of the workforce. At the same time that we've been carrying out these efforts to reduce unnecessary system involvement, we've also been strengthening our child protective work and the vital effort to protect children from maltreatment and abuse. It is critical that our child protective staff have the tools and skills needed to identify those children truly in danger and connect families to services and supports

and foster care if necessary so children can be safe. We have significantly reduced child protective caseloads to 7.6, which is well below national standards and enables CPS to have the time to provide each family with the attention they deserve. In the summer of '24, we added staff and units to the Family Preservation Program, which is an intensive child protection prevention model that enables children to remain safely at home while ACS works with the family to address immediate child safety concerns. FPP helps families by accompanying them to appointments, helping them navigate systems such as housing and school, and arranging for services such as homemaking or heavy duty cleaning. We've also made sure that our CPS have access to those with expertise so they have the tools they need to best assess safety. For example, in the highest risk cases, CPS have coaches and access to investigative consultants who are former NYPD as well as child advocacy centers to help assess for abuse. In January, we launched our new clinical support program where licensed professional support frontline child protective staff with their expertise in mental health, substance abuse, and intimate partner violence. Through this newly

enhanced program, this team of experts now engages directly with families and offers hands-on support and connections to services specific to each family's needs. We also have a number of quality assurance mechanisms in place to help us continually assess our practice and make enhancements when we see they are warranted. ChildStat is a weekly meeting focused on safety practice and child protection by looking at both data and randomly selected active cases from a different child protection borough each week. The panel includes myself and other leadership from across the agency, typically with 700 plus staff in attendance, and is broadcast across the agency, promoting a culture of continuous learning and shared accountability. In 2025, we launched a new multidisciplinary review panel to bring experts external to ACS into our fatality review process to help identify systemic solutions to enhance ACS's ability to protect children and deliver high-quality services. This panel gives us a formal pathway to incorporate the expertise of members such as those with lived experience and experts in mental health,

substance abuse, homelessness, law enforcement, etc., into our policy and practice. The panel also aims to help New Yorkers better understand our work as we promote transparency and system accountability. We will be incorporating the panel's recommendations into our annual fatality reports released each June. Another area where we see disparity is the length of time children spend in foster care. Black and Hispanic children placed in foster care are significantly more likely than White children in care to return home within their first year of placement, but once they've been in care for a full year or more, Black and Hispanic children are about 25 percent less likely to go home during that second or later year. We've got to talk as to why it took five years for me to, from beginning to adoption. For me, it took five years, in and out of court. I don't ever want that to happen to another parent who mean well, who wants to foster and then adopt the boys, but it took five years in my case, from beginning to end, until I got the boys. We don't want to see that, and that's why I'm asking what kind of reforms you're doing around that length, because I know after 18 months, the State is supposed to come in and start looking for permanency and all of that. I did all of that, twice. I did two sets of 18 months before I finally got the boys. I want to prevent that from the beginning for any parent who means well, who wants to take in children, but five years is a long… I ran out of days as a teacher, because I went back and forth to court so many times.
Definitely, we can make time to talk and hear more and figure out the missteps and make sure they're not repeated.

When you do reunification with parents, what kind of support do you provide when that child go back into the house?

Is there mental health support for everyone when that child re-enters that family?

With reunification, it's almost like a two-step process. Agencies are preparing families for reunification, so that's where they're assessing. Maybe that's when we're moving to overnight visits, and they're doing that kind of work ahead of time. The Commissioner discussed the discharge grant, because while reunification is a time where the child and their parents are coming back together, there's financial needs. The discharge grant was recently increased to 2,000 dollars per child, and that will help the parents plan for the children. The child may have left. They were two. They had one size bed. Now maybe they're three. They need a bigger bed. They need more furniture. They need additional clothes. That, to me, releases the stress. They don't have to worry about the finances, so that's one aspect. Then when they are reunified, we have trial discharge, so agencies are still expected to provide service planning, case planning, make casework contacts, assess how that trial period is going. They report back to the court. We have family team conferences that ACS facilitates

prior to trial discharge and prior to final discharge to make sure the family is in a good place to close out the case. To answer your question, yes, the service plan will remain the same, so if it's counseling, if the child needs counseling, maybe this is the time where family counseling is introduced. There's information that they're gathering just to make sure everything is steady, things are going well. The goal of trial discharge is to help continue to provide as many services the family needs. We often may make referrals to prevention at that time to continue to support the family.

And I know at one point, I know you are now currently in public schools with a preventive. Do you plan to expand? Because I know that's one of the things Council Member Stevens and I talk about. We want prevention before a case happens. We want to make sure the supports are in place for parents and families. Do you plan to expand, and how is that going, and how many schools, just off the top of my head, I can't remember, how many schools are you in, and do you plan to expand the program until more families are aware of this?

A couple things. One is there's 16 contracts that serve about three schools each, so it's just under 50 schools. It's going well. They're just launched. There's no expansion plan yet, but we've seen a lot more families access services. And as I mentioned in my testimony, we created this kind of pilot to test a capacity for, to give providers resources to be able to serve families with concrete needs and other supports without opening a prevention case, because obviously we've heard very often that folks don't want to be a case, and so we're looking at all ways we can do that. We've expanded the Family Enrichment Center. There's also, I think, both in the mental health space and generally in family support, we want to be supportive of initiatives outside of the ACS continuum, and so this work that we're doing with the Health Department to help them expand NFPX, the work that many advocates are doing to re-envision some family wellbeing work, that's all conversation we think is really important in this domain, whether it's within the ACS continuum or outside of it.

I know we're talking about the harm caused by ACS. How do we look

back for the families that were harmed 50 years ago? How do we go back and fix a lot of that harm that was done to communities of color?

Yeah. So, as I mentioned earlier, there's about 50,000 children in foster care in 1996. There's been a lot of work to change that. Related to harm that has been committed, harm that is continuing to happen, I think I really appreciate Commissioner Tigani's testimony. I think we have to have ways to come together to have different structures, whether that's the accountability council or some other way. My hope is that it's very diverse experiences with ACS are represented. Absolutely young people, absolutely families, parents. About 7 percent of families experience of investigations, about 7 percent go to family court, and so we know there's lots of different experiences. We also know that intrusion unnecessarily is a very harmful thing. And I think something that I've tried to bring to this work in all my conversations with the team and all of the ways in which we're leading is you can do great, you can make absolute strides and change people's lives to the positive, or you can do harm in this work,

whether that's a young person who's unsafe, whether that's a family that's disrespected. I really appreciate my staff who put themselves at that nexus and try to get it right. We have a huge responsibility and whatever we do harm, it has to be acknowledged, whether that's historical or current.
Thank you, Chair.

Thank you, Council Member Joseph. My next question is, neglect reported by schools called by educator reporters are far less likely to be substantiated than calls by other mandated reporters in New York City, and calls by education reported that alleged neglect only were substantiated 89 percent of the time in 2023. More than 82 percent of the children in those reports are Black and Latino. ACS has trained 1,300 educators that can directly support families instead of making a report, and education reporters' calls have come down 90 percent since 2023. However, educators still called the hotlines 10,000 times in 2025. What is ACS learning about education report calls, particularly related to neglect, and how schools can more often directly link families to resources?

I think there's two important things here. One is that we've learned. One is that the fear associated with not calling is real. That is, whether that's concern about criminal liability, whether that's concern about liability related to licensure, or even just sort of in community. The other piece is that folks didn't know enough about where to get help other than, so it was, we have the situation, let's call the SCR. And I think our message used to be, when in doubt, let us figure it out. And so, at the same time, more than half of the calls from schools are not education neglect only. And so, they involve concerns about potential abuse, they concern a number of different other factors. So, we want schools to call when they feel a child is in danger, and we want them to get help when they think a family needs support, and they are well positioned, and I really, really appreciate our colleagues at New York City Public Schools, because they've taken this on as their mandate. They're really well positioned to help. The State has made a couple changes, which is that when they call for education neglect only, they ask the school, what have you done, and so, have you sent anybody out,

have you tried to solve this problem, have you provided resources, and I think that's been an important part in reducing the calls as well.

Yeah. I think that piece is so important, because so often it's like, how did you contribute to this, or did you find out any more information, so, I think that is important. The next question I have is also, and Council Member Joseph kind of hit on this as well, is the school-based early support program. And I know this is something you've been championing, and I'm really excited about having. Have you seen schools making use of this program, and could you talk a little bit about what this has been like from this launch? What are some of the things that you've seen to help support this, and the vision behind it?

Yeah. It's been really encouraging, and thank you to Deputy Commissioner Linares for her leadership around this. We have seen about a 20 percent increase in families accessing services, if you look at the last six months compared to six months previously. And over the last few years, we've seen from about 10 percent to 25 percent of families accessing preventive

services voluntarily, not through a child protective route. And when they do, their records are protected. They sit at the non-profits. They're not in the ACS system of record, so it doesn't become part of a potential subsequent child protective investigation, and it's important families see that protection. They're called advocates cases because the advocates sued a quarter century ago to protect that from being within the child protective system, and it's something that New York City should be really proud of. Each non-profit has been engaging schools. We've had lots of success, trying to really make sure that they know how to access the support through school-based early support. I would also say, where there were challenges in the beginning, and sort of understanding that our New York City Public Schools partners were really great to try to help us work with the principals, work with the superintendents. Each of the superintendents had to sign off on the contract being submitted, and then we had to really drill that down with the principals. There's very regular convenings that we have with the schools and with the providers together to make sure that we're solving all those issues.

And with the 50 schools that this program is in, were you guys looking at areas where there were high numbers of reports, or how was the demographics broken up? Were there a lot of calls in that school?
Yeah.
Were you just looking at poverty rates? How was that determined?

It was rates of poverty, it was rates of calls to ACS, it was rates of unemployment, a whole host of things. And Winette is telling me that we've had 1,077 families who are served through that model so far.
And have you seen a decrease in those areas that the schools are in now because they have this new service?
I think it's too early to say, to see, you know, we can take a look. I don't think an evaluation would be primed yet. We're still in the first year of it, but that's the goal.

And so even with the, thinking about even the enrichment centers, and thinking about, because they've been, I know the

expansion happened, it's been like a year or so. Have we seen a decline in those communities as well, with the presence of enrichment centers in those communities?
We've been doing so many…
And I know all of them haven't opened, so I know.

Yeah, but we've been taking down lots of, you know, obviously we've seen this decrease in the scope of the child protective system, and it's across the city. I think we've been doing a lot of different things at once, and so I don't think we're yet positioned to attribute it to one initiative or another, because we have about a dozen things that we've talked about going on at the same time, but it's something we're really curious about figuring out.
Yeah. You came in with a lot of ideas, so.
Well, I had a lot of people in my ear, some behind me.

Listen, we appreciate it.

Truancy and other attendance issues reported as educational neglect in New York Times reported in two pieces last week, half of the state did not have educational neglect in their stature, meaning that child protection is not called when children are absent from school. What is ACS learning from the nature of educational neglect reports specifically through CARES cases, and what might ACS see in the next steps in City efforts to address attendance issues without a child protective response?

Yeah, I think a few things. One is, in educational neglect cases only, whether it's CARES or a child protective investigation, we really try to understand what the root cause is. Sometimes there are challenges with young people's behavior, lack of access to services. Sometimes there is mental health challenges for the parents. Sometimes there's a combination. And so, we really try to understand what services can help. We try to do meetings with the school to see if we can work something out. Sometimes it's an inappropriate school placement, or an IEP hasn't been done, or there's school phobia. There really is not a single

one, which is why we have to make sure we understand and do a careful assessment.

CARES is an alternative response to child welfare investigation for low and moderate risk reported concerns of child abuse and maltreatment. Can you explain why CARES is a core strategy for combating racial disparities?

Yeah. I think it's key because if we can solve a problem without having a family have an indication of maltreatment, even if there has been some concern, that is not going to saddle them with an economic hardship where they can't get certain jobs. When a young person is not going to school and the parent has not been able to express a minimum degree of care in that moment, if we can help them get, in some cases we see parents who are experiencing depression or going through some trauma themselves. We want to make sure we can help families without then making it harder for them to do well. The indication or unsubstantiation is an administrative decision. It doesn't really drive the next steps. I think it's a tool that I think we should really be examining because it doesn't indicate just because there's an indication you have

to go to court. The real question is what's the risk and how do you mitigate it in the least intrusive way? That's the goal that we are trying to rally around. One of the reasons I think CARES eliminates that indication or not conversation and allows for more trust and more conversation to be had because families don't have to have fear that they're going to get that indication if they tell a story that might include some mistakes.

According to ACS data in FY 2025, White and Asian families were referred to CARES at higher rates than Black and Latinx children. What strategy or mechanisms is ACS considering to address this disparity?

It's pretty close, but we've got to narrow it even further. We look at this in ChildStat constantly. We look by allegation, by race. We think there's some difference in allegation by race, and CARES is driven by allegation, so there are certain things you cannot go down the CARES track with if they're alleged. We're trying to narrow that gap to make sure we're looking geographically. It's one of the key indicators in our CARES ChildStat work, and we're

always trying to examine with each borough, each neighborhood, each zone to make sure we understand the distribution. A lot of this, the determination for CARES is a few steps. The State labels it FAR eligible, Family Assessment Response. We call it CARES here in New York City. It's then looked at by our applications team, which does a quick look at the allegation and the history, and then it is initially tracked down one way or the other. You can go back from an investigation to CARES within the first seven days, so we're also working with staff to identify places where that initial track towards an investigation could be re-evaluated.

In New York State, hotline screens for far fewer calls than most states, which contributes to high investigation rates of New York City's for Black and Latino families. This suggests that many CARES cases would not be referred to children protective responses in other states. What types of cases does the agency believe could be handled in other ways? For instance, materials needed in hardships, ACS investigators, frequently fined food assistants, baby supplies including cribs, strollers, diapers, clothes, child care vouchers, and

connected to benefits and screening for parents. How might stronger community pathways to family supports prevent ACS involvement? I know a lot, even with the enrichment centers, that is something that you guys have really been using to create community solutions, but are there other things that we should be looking to do to try to just kind of help? I know CORE mentioned a universal basic income, or are there other things that you think should be implemented?

I think every way we can help families have the security that they need, we should be pursuing. At the State level, I know there's a lot of conversation about reforming the SCR, and OCFS is very engaged in that. I think one thing that we could do is to create a state law that allows for local discretion around having cases be closed before the seven-day period. Often, especially around malicious reports, someone can call, make an allegation, we might have been in the home two days before, there might be a series of malicious allegations. The work that we have to do, sometimes we call the State and say, can you take this back, but they have to make the decision by current law, sort of based on the allegation, if it

was true, if it was credible, it would constitute maltreatment. We sometimes know a lot more than they do. If we had that discretion at a local level, our idea, and we've been talking to various folks around that, would be to create, in state law, the capacity for localities to have that discretion, and then maybe have localities submit a plan to the State like we do for CARES. They created discretion around different tracks. This could be almost a third track. If we got a very similar call to something we've just investigated, we don't believe the credibility of the caller, maybe we do a virtual visit, and then we close it out, or maybe we pursue support in a different way. I think New York City needs more discretion in that regard.

That's a good recommendation. We'll definitely note that. What is the current budget for preventive services, and how has it changed since 2021's foster care redesign? Could you provide context on any shifts in funding priorities or allocation over this period, and what aspects of preventive services are the most costly?

So, I'll get the exact number, I forgot I was in a budget hearing, so it's 300 million dollars plus. But we have been doing a lot of work in preventive services actually to examine the whole system. Last year, we took a look at chronic underutilization, where families really were not voting with their feet to access those family support services. We took that down, but we reinvested that money into helping non-profits on workforce, and helping non-profits meet concrete needs. The most expensive of the preventive services are the treatment modalities that are evidence-based. But we've been putting more and more money in services that are most accessible.

According to 2025 data, despite representing a significant share of SCR intakes, Black children account for a smaller share of preventive services cases opening. What criteria guides referrals to preventive services, and how does ACS ensure the criteria are applied equitably?

Yeah. I mean, this is something that is less about the referral differences, and more about families where they want to get services. And so, we more often see Black

families wanting to get services from community-based organizations, from where they trust in the community, and not have an ongoing preventive services case. This is something we're trying. It's one of the reasons we are extending this different type of preventive service, where you do not have to open a case through the school-based early support process, but we really do want to respect family voice and agency. We got to make sure our services are ones that folks trust and are strong. And so, we're seeing this new wave around more and more voluntary families coming to preventive services, which we're encouraged by, but we do want to make sure if a family has a community that can support them, we shouldn't override that.

Yeah, no. I mean, absolutely we shouldn't, but, you know, we want to make sure that it's not a repeat thing, and so, how do we keep track of that, so I would love for us to think about, well, not you, but us, the rest of us, figure out how to keep track of that. Because I think it is important for us to make sure that, yes, they can say they're going to get the services, but what does the follow-up look like?
And, Chair, if I may, just the last year's, 372.4 million is in prevention services.
